opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think internal deployment is one of the most underrated parts of the risk picture right now. A lot of the public conversation focuses on external deployment, meaning what happens when a model gets released to customers through an API or a chat product. But the most capable systems in the world are typically used inside the labs first, often for months, and sometimes they never get released at all. And the way they're used internally is often much more high-stakes than how they're used externally.

Think about what these models are actually doing inside a frontier company. Increasingly they're writing code, running experiments, and helping with AI research itself. They might have access to the company's codebase, its compute infrastructure, potentially even the training pipelines for the next generation of models. So if a model has misaligned goals, or is scheming in some way, the internal environment is exactly where it would have the most leverage. It's also where you'd get the kind of fast feedback loop people worry about, AI accelerating AI R&D, with fewer outside eyes on it.

So what should companies do? A few things.

First, treat internal deployment as a deployment decision in its own right. Right now many safety frameworks are mostly triggered at the point of external release. I think the same kind of evaluations, especially for dangerous capabilities and for things like scheming propensity, should happen before a model is broadly rolled out internally, not just before it goes public.

Second, think carefully about access and permissions. The default shouldn't be that a new, more capable model gets the same broad access to systems that the previous one had. You want something like least privilege: what does this model actually need for this task? Can it modify its own training setup? Can it touch monitoring infrastructure? Those should be deliberate choices.

Third, monitoring. If you're running agents internally at scale, you want logging and automated monitoring of what they're doing, including their reasoning where you can see it, so you can catch suspicious behavior like sandbagging, trying to disable oversight, or acquiring resources it doesn't need. This is basically the AI control agenda: assume the model might not be trustworthy, and design your setup so that even if it isn't, it can't cause catastrophic harm without getting caught.

Fourth, internal security against humans too. Insider risk is real, both people misusing a very capable model and model weights getting exfiltrated.

And finally, some degree of transparency and external oversight. At the moment, the public and governments have very little visibility into what's running inside labs. I don't think every detail needs to be public, but I'd like to see companies share with governments, or trusted third parties, what their most capable internal systems can do and what safeguards are in place. Otherwise we could end up in a world where the most important AI developments happen entirely behind closed doors, and the first time anyone outside hears about a problem is when it's already too late to do much about it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends reviewing permissions and access needs, but it does not clearly recommend assessing deployment risks against the company’s specific security and access configuration.

r002.rationale: It recommends least privilege and says a new model should not automatically receive the previous model’s broad access; access should depend on what the task requires.

r003.rationale: It says internal deployment should be treated as a deployment decision and recommends applying safety evaluations before broad internal rollout.

r004.rationale: It says the most capable systems are used inside labs first, describes internal AI research as a fast feedback loop, and characterizes internal use as higher stakes than external use.

r005.rationale: It says a scheming model would have the most leverage in the internal environment and frames internal use of the most capable systems as preceding external release.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think internal deployment is actually one of the most underrated parts of this whole picture. Everyone focuses on the public release, the moment a model goes out to millions of users, and there's a lot of scrutiny there. But the first place these systems get used in a really serious way is inside the companies themselves. They're used to write code, to help with research, increasingly to accelerate the next generation of models. And that happens months before anyone outside sees the system, often with far fewer safeguards.

So the first thing I'd say is: treat internal deployment as a deployment. That sounds obvious, but in practice a lot of labs have historically thought of it as "we're just testing," and the policies and evaluations kick in only when something goes external. I think the right frame is that if a model has access to your codebase, your compute, your internal tools, and it's being used by hundreds of employees, that is a real deployment with real risks, and it should go through a comparable process.

Concretely, I'd want a few things. One is dangerous capability evaluations that actually gate internal use, not just external release. If a model is capable enough that you'd be worried about it autonomously exfiltrating weights or sabotaging research, then those evals should run before it gets broad access internally, because internally is exactly where it has the most opportunity to do those things.

The second is control measures. So this is the idea that even if you can't fully trust the model, you design the environment so that it can't cause catastrophic harm. Things like monitoring the actions the model takes, having a trusted, weaker model or a human review high-stakes actions, limiting permissions, logging everything. The analogy I like is insider threat: companies already have processes for the possibility that an employee might be compromised or malicious. You should have similar processes for a model that might be scheming or just misaligned in ways you haven't detected.

Third, I think there needs to be a lot more transparency about this. Right now, nobody outside a lab really knows how capable the internally deployed models are, how they're being used, or what safeguards exist. I'd like to see companies publish at least high-level information: here's what we're using these systems for, here's the level of autonomy they have, here are the controls in place. And ideally, there's some external party, a government body or an independent auditor, that gets a deeper look.

And the fourth, which I think is the hardest one, is the governance question. When a model is being used to accelerate AI research itself, you get this feedback loop where internal deployment speeds up the next model, which gets deployed internally, and so on. The competitive pressure to just keep going is enormous. So I think companies need commitments made in advance about what capability thresholds would cause them to pause or add safeguards, because in the moment, every incentive points toward "just ship it internally, it's fine."

I want to be fair here. Some labs have started taking this seriously, and some of the frontier safety frameworks do mention internal deployment now. But I'd say we're still early. The gap between how much scrutiny external release gets and how much internal use gets is, in my view, one of the bigger blind spots in the current safety landscape.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risks from access to code, compute, and tools, but does not recommend assessing risks against each company’s specific security and access configuration.

r002.rationale: It recommends limiting permissions, but does not clearly say systems should receive access only when necessary rather than by default.

r003.rationale: It recommends treating internal use as a real deployment, with policies and evaluations applying before broad internal access, and notes that frontier safety frameworks should address internal deployment.

r004.rationale: It says serious internal use happens before public release, but does not clearly predict that AI R&D risks will initially arise largely from internal rather than external deployment.

r005.rationale: It identifies internal access as an opportunity for models that may scheme, but does not clearly predict that scheming risks will initially arise largely from internal rather than external deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to treat internal deployment as a deployment. There’s sometimes this implicit assumption that if a model isn’t available to the public, then it’s safe. But internally you might be giving it access to your codebase, your model weights, your research infrastructure—and potentially quite a lot of autonomy. So the relevant question is: what can it actually do, and what would happen if it behaved in a way you didn’t intend?

I’d want companies to start with limited permissions, sandbox the system where possible, and require human approval for consequential actions. You can then expand access as you get evidence that the safeguards work. And you should be logging and monitoring what the system does, so that you can investigate suspicious behaviour and stop a deployment if necessary.

One important distinction is between trusting the model and building a setup that doesn’t require so much trust. If your safety case is essentially, ‘We’ve asked it not to do anything bad, and so far it’s been helpful,’ that’s pretty weak. You want to test whether it could bypass your controls, whether your monitoring would catch that, and whether the people overseeing it have enough information to intervene.

And this becomes particularly important when models are helping with AI research itself. There are real benefits there, including for safety research. But the pressure to give them more access and run them faster is going to be very strong. So you want clear criteria for expanding their role—and clear conditions for pausing—before you’re relying on them heavily.

r001.rationale: It recommends evaluating what a system can do and what could happen based on its access to company assets and its autonomy.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with limited permissions and expanding access only as evidence supports the safeguards.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend explicitly covering internal deployment in frontier safety policies.

r004.rationale: It does not predict that AI R&D risks will initially arise largely from internal deployment.

r005.rationale: It does not predict that AI scheming risks will initially arise largely from internal deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to recognise that internal deployment is still deployment. If a model has access to your codebase, your research infrastructure, or credentials that let it take actions, then the fact that it’s only being used by employees doesn’t automatically make it safe.

So I’d want companies to be quite explicit about what the model can access and what it can do. Can it run experiments? Can it change code? Can it communicate externally? And then you want safeguards that are appropriate to those permissions: sandboxing, limited access, logging, and human approval for particularly consequential actions.

One concern is that you gradually give models more autonomy because they’re useful, and no individual step feels like a big decision. But eventually you’ve built a system that can do quite a lot with relatively little oversight. You want to assess that whole setup, rather than just asking whether the underlying model passed an evaluation before you deployed it.

And I’d want the monitoring and security measures to be tested adversarially. If a model were trying to evade oversight or get access to something it shouldn’t, would you actually catch it? You shouldn’t assume that a human nominally being in the loop is sufficient, especially if that human is reviewing more work than they can realistically understand.

r001.rationale: The response recommends assessing the whole setup, including what the model can access and do, and tailoring safeguards to those permissions.

r002.rationale: It recommends limited access but does not clearly say access should be granted only when necessary rather than by default.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend covering internal deployment in frontier safety policies.

r004.rationale: It makes no prediction comparing where AI R&D risks will initially arise.

r005.rationale: It makes no prediction comparing where AI scheming risks will initially arise.
